method: Each section read in full by a machine-assisted reviewer against the packs and the ground catalogue as of this date; not a legal review.

sections.bearsOn: Defines claim, lease, mineral title, recorded holder, mining activity, mineral lands, mineral and placer mineral (sand, gravel, earth and soil are not minerals, so a road gravel pit is not under this Act) and construction purpose (road building and fill).
Regulations may prescribe a rock or substance as, or not as, a mineral; no compensation follows.
The chief gold commissioner designates mining divisions.
Appointment of the chief gold commissioner, gold commissioners and inspectors, who may enter titled land.
Certified copies of registry records are evidence; how notices are given.
Searching the registry.
The Electronic Transactions Act applies to the online registry.
The mineral titles online registry, from which the mineral tenure layer the screen reads is published.

Claim and lease changes take effect on registration.
Applications to convert claims to leases.
Abandoning a claim or surrendering a lease by registered discharge.
Registering transfers of claims and leases.

Suspending registry functions.

Registration priority by time of payment.
Registration by other means to avoid hardship.
Only a free miner may hold a claim or lease.
Issue of free miner certificates.
Recreational hand panning, not on a title without the holder's permission.
Suspension or cancellation of a free miner certificate for contraventions, including of the Heritage Conservation Act.

A free miner may enter mineral lands, Crown forest land included, to explore, but not land under cultivation, occupied buildings, heritage property or parks; a block over mineral lands remains open to exploration entry.

A recorded holder with a Mines Act permit must, with the Chief Inspector's approval, be issued a special use permit for access to the title for exploration; it governs a mining road's authority, not a forest road's.
Claims and leases are distinct titles.
The chief gold commissioner decides disputes between recorded holders and holders of mineral substance rights.

A recorded holder may use, enter and occupy the surface of a claim or lease for exploration and production once any Mines Act permit is issued, and on request is issued a free use permit or occupant licence to cut for the timber; a land use designation or objective does not preclude its applications except in parks, ecological reserves, ELUA no-mining areas and designated Land Act areas.
The Land Act minister must dispose of surface rights on unreserved, unoccupied Crown land to a mining lease holder when the minister certifies they are required for mining.

Land Act acquisitions applied for before a claim have priority; a later disposition of surface rights over a valid mineral title does not diminish the holder's rights except as an order of the chief gold commissioner or minister, a Surface Rights Board settlement or a quit claim agreement determines.

The minister may by order restrict surface rights or mineral rights in a title where the surface holds a cultural heritage resource or should be used for purposes other than mining; such an order is what would settle a conflict between a claim and forest use.
Compensation when Park Act s. 11 expropriates a claim or lease.
The chief gold commissioner may order compliance, suspend operations and cancel a claim for contraventions.

Before a mining activity, notice must be served on private surface owners and Land Act lease and disposition holders, who are compensated for loss; disputes go to the Surface Rights Board. Forest tenure holders are not listed.
